description: Our mission is to empower farming communities and agricultural organizations by seamlessly integrating advanced NASA Earth observations and local soil data into their daily operations.
summary:
Leyar Shift helps the farmer to work out what to grow next. You plot your field on the satellite map and tell it how the field is watered, what machinery you have, what's most important to you and what you're growing at the moment. It then takes your current rotation and compares it to the others that are appropriate for that field. It then presents the best option alongside what you're growing at the moment in terms of water requirement, income (in your own currency) and the number of days per year that bad weather would put the crop at risk.

Every answer is derived from the data for that particular field: 25 years of daily NASA POWER weather, GPM IMERG rainfall, GRACE and GRACE-FO water storage, GLDAS and NLDAS soil water, MODIS and Sentinel-2 greenness and NASADEM elevation. Each rotation goes through 500 weather years so every number has an honest range. It works for any field on the planet, on a phone.

Groundwater is falling under many farms. Near Ludhiana, Punjab, GRACE shows the water stored under the region dropping about 4 cm a year, and Leyar Shift finds a rotation that needs about 83% less pumped water. On a Kansas corn pivot, its water estimate matches OpenET's satellite measurement within about 1%.
details:
Leyar Shift takes its name from the Burmese word လယ်ယာ (le yar), meaning farmland: the paddy fields and upland farms that feed Myanmar.

Leyar Shift is a web app that helps a farmer choose their next crop rotation. The farmer marks a field on a satellite map, or types its size and drops a square. They say how it gets water, what equipment they have, what matters most to them (saving water, income, soil health and so on), and what they grow now. In the United States it reads the current rotation from the USDA crop map; anywhere else the farmer enters it, year by year.

The engine then collects data for that exact field. It reads 25 years of daily NASA POWER weather, GPM IMERG rainfall through NASA Giovanni, GLDAS and NLDAS soil water, and GRACE and GRACE-FO water storage. Greenness comes from MODIS and Sentinel-2, and elevation from NASADEM. Soil comes from the USDA soil survey or ISRIC SoilGrids. In the US it adds USDA yields and prices, USGS wells and OpenET water use. It runs an FAO-56 daily water balance for every rotation that suits the field, through 500 weather years. It then scores each one on water needed, soil health, soil washing away, risk from bad weather, breaking pest cycles and income, weighted by the farmer's own priorities. The screen shows each step live while it works.

The result puts the best fit next to what the farmer grows now: water needed, income in the local currency, and days of weather risk, with a range on every number. When two rotations are about equal, it says so instead of picking a winner. When data is missing, it says what is missing and why rather than filling the gap with a guess. Every number names its source, and the Resources page links the data sources behind it.

We checked it against independent measurements. On a Kansas corn pivot, its water use matches OpenET's satellite estimate within about 1% (915 against 919 mm a year). Near Ludhiana, Punjab, GRACE shows the water stored under the region falling about 4 cm a year, and the tool finds a rotation there that needs about 83% less pumped water.

The intended impact is better rotation decisions where water is running short, made with evidence a farmer can read on a phone. The tool supports the farmer's judgment; it does not replace it, and it suggests checking key points with a local agronomist.

What makes it different: it compares whole rotations rather than single crops, sets them against the farmer's own rotation rather than an ideal one, and checks its model against satellite and ground data.

Built with Python (FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio, Shapely, pyproj) and TypeScript (React, Vite, MapLibre GL), hosted on Vercel, with automated browser and engine tests. AI coding assistants helped write, review and debug parts of the code and wording; every number on screen comes from the engine, not from a language model. All data, photos and video we used are credited, and their sources are listed in this submission.
